title: Three Newborns Die in NICU Fire at Government Hospital in Amravati, Maharashtra
excerpt: A ventilator explosion triggered a blaze in the neonatal intensive care unit of a government hospital in Amravati. Chief Minister Fadnavis has ordered a high-level inquiry.
body:
• Three newborn babies died after a fire broke out in the neonatal intensive care unit of a government hospital in Amravati, Maharashtra.
  • The blaze was reportedly triggered by a ventilator blast in the NICU, according to initial reports from officials.
  • Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis has ordered a high-level inquiry into the incident and announced Rs 5 lakh compensation for the victims' families.
  • The tragedy highlights persistent fire safety concerns in Indian government hospitals, following similar incidents in Bhandara (2021), Bhopal, and most recently Chhindwara.

Ventilator Blast Triggers Fatal Blaze

Three newborn babies lost their lives after a fire broke out in the neonatal intensive care unit of a government hospital in Amravati, eastern Maharashtra. The blaze was reportedly triggered by a ventilator explosion in the NICU, officials said.

https://x.com/NewsArenaIndia/status/2091729604025495553

Hospital staff noticed smoke emanating from the neonatal unit and immediately alerted fire services. Fire tenders were dispatched to the scene, but the three infants sustained fatal injuries before they could be rescued. Other newborns in the unit were evacuated and shifted to nearby facilities.

Eyewitness accounts from parents at the hospital described harrowing scenes. One parent recalled seeing infants covered in ashes as the fire engulfed the ward, according to reports from The New Indian Express.

Fadnavis Orders High-Level Inquiry

Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis responded swiftly, ordering a high-level inquiry into the fire and the safety conditions at the hospital. The state government announced immediate compensation of Rs 5 lakh for each of the victims' families.

District authorities have set up an investigative committee to determine the exact cause of the fire and assess whether safety protocols were followed. Preliminary indications point to a malfunction in the ventilator equipment, though a definitive conclusion awaits the formal investigation.

The incident has prompted calls for a comprehensive audit of fire safety systems and medical equipment maintenance across government hospitals in the state.

A Pattern of Hospital Fire Tragedies

The Amravati fire is the latest in a disturbing pattern of hospital fire incidents across India, particularly in neonatal care units where vulnerable infants rely on electrical life-support equipment.

In January 2021, ten newborn babies died after a fire broke out in the Special Newborn Care Unit at the district general hospital in Bhandara, also in eastern Maharashtra. That fire was attributed to a short circuit in an air conditioner. Then-opposition leader Fadnavis had demanded strict action and a thorough probe at the time.

Just days before the Amravati incident, three newborns suffered severe burn injuries after a radiant warmer machine caught fire in the NICU of Chhindwara District Hospital in Madhya Pradesh on August 22. Those infants were rushed to Jabalpur for emergency surgical intervention.

In November 2024, ten newborn babies were killed in a hospital fire in Uttar Pradesh, where fire alarms in the intensive care unit failed to activate during the blaze. Multiple previous incidents at hospitals in Bhopal and other cities have similarly exposed critical gaps in fire safety infrastructure at government medical facilities.

Systemic Safety Concerns

Healthcare safety advocates have long warned about inadequate fire safety measures in India's public hospital system. Equipment maintenance protocols, electrical safety audits, and emergency evacuation procedures remain inconsistent across state-run facilities.

The recurring nature of these tragedies has drawn scrutiny from courts, civil society organizations, and political leaders. After the Bhandara fire, Maharashtra's then-Deputy Chief Minister Ajit Pawar ordered a fire safety audit of all government and private hospitals in the state, but compliance has remained uneven.

The Amravati investigation is expected to examine whether the hospital's fire safety equipment was functional, when it was last inspected, and whether the NICU's electrical systems met safety standards for critical medical equipment.
nri_angle: Hospital safety standards in India remain a pressing concern for NRI families with relatives relying on public healthcare, and these recurring tragedies fuel calls for systemic reform.
